column6: Rational Turán exponents of a single $k$-uniform hypergraph
column7: For a fixed $k$-uniform hypergraph $F$, let $\mathrm{ex}_k(n,F)$ denote the maximum number of edges in an $F$-free $k$-uniform hypergraph on $n$ vertices. We prove that for every integer $k\ge2$ and every rational $r\in[0,1]$ there exists a $k$-uniform hypergraph $F_{k,r}$ such that \begin{equation*} \mathrm{ex}_k(n,F_{k,r})=Θ(n^{k-r}). \end{equation*} The case $k=2$ is the rational exponents conjecture of Erdős and Simonovits \cite{Erdos1988}, also known as Erdős problem \#571 \cite{BloomErdoswebsite}; a proof was announced in September 2026 and is expounded by Conlon et al.\ \cite{Conlon-Janzer-Jiang-Kim-Lee-Liu-Longbrake-Yepremyan}. For $k\ge3$ the theorem extends their result to $k$-uniform hypergraphs. In the single-hypergraph setting, this strengthens Fitch's finite-family theorem \cite{Fitch} by realizing each exponent with a single forbidden $k$-uniform hypergraph for $0\le r\le1$. We also show, via an explicit two-edge construction, that for $k\ge4$ this strengthening fails for $\lceil k/2\rceil<r\le k-1$: no single $k$-uniform hypergraph $F$ then satisfies $\mathrm{ex}_k(n,F)=Θ(n^{k-r})$. The main result of this paper has been formalized in Lean 4, conditional on two explicitly stated axioms.

column6: Size Ramsey numbers of star forests with two components on one side
column7: We determine the size Ramsey number of a two-component star forest versus an arbitrary star forest. Let $q,a,b,n_1,\ldots,n_q$ be positive integers with $a\ge b$ and $n_1\ge\cdots\ge n_q$. We prove that \[ \begin{split} \rhat\left(K_{1,a}\sq K_{1,b}, \bigsqcup_{i=1}^{q}K_{1,n_i}\right) ={}&(a+n_1-1) +\sum_{i=1}^{q-1}\max\{a+n_{i+1}-1,b+n_i-1\}\\ &+(b+n_q-1). \end{split} \] This proves the conjecture of Burr, Erdős, Faudree, Rousseau and Schelp (Erdős Problem~\#561) in the case where one of the two star forests has exactly two components. The formula holds without any restriction on the parity of the star sizes. The proof combines vertex deletion, iterated matching deletion, and Lovász's factor theorem.

column5: Stijn Cambie; Denis Paliy; Rafał Wrona
column6: Short Proofs for the Minimum Number of Determined Circles
column7: We present short proofs for the main parts of the recently completed solution of Erdős Problem 506, which asks for the minimum number of distinct circles determined by a finite planar point set that is neither collinear nor concyclic. An inversion argument and a seven-point line lemma show that eight points determine at least $17$ circles, and an explicit configuration attains this bound. A single argument combining Melchior's inequality with Langer's incidence bound establishes the sharp formula for every $n\ge15$. The proofs give concise alternatives to longer arguments in the recent literature; the remaining finite cases are cited separately.

column5: Kanghyeon Kim; Johannes F. Lutzeyer; Yanzhu Guo
column6: Attention-Graph Curvature for the Verification of Mathematical Reasoning
column7: Language models have recently solved open Erdős problems and achieved gold-medal level performance on International Mathematical Olympiad problems. But their solutions, written in natural language, cannot yet be verified by proof assistants. An erroneous reasoning step can invalidate every step that comes after, so it is advantageous to detect errors early. Several methods have been proposed to detect erroneous reasoning quickly based on the features of the forward pass of the language model that performs reasoning. In this work, we study whether the directed Forman curvature of that model's attention graph, a local quantity computed at an edge from the attention weights around it, carries information about a step's correctness. To do so, we evaluate four per-step verifiers on ProcessBench with and without the curvature appended to their input. Appending curvature values improves the overall mean performance of all four verifiers. ReProbe, the verifier that takes every token of a step as input, shows the largest improvement. Adding the curvature increases the time of the language model's forward pass by 18% on average. Our code is available at https://github.com/kanghyeonz/attention-graph-curvature.

column6: Coprime pairs with equal sum of divisors, assuming smooth shifted primes
column7: Let $h(x)$ be the number of pairs $1\le a<b<x$ with $\gcd(a,b)=1$ and $σ(a)=σ(b)$. Erdős Problem #824 asks whether $h(x)>x^{2-o(1)}$. By an argument of Pollack and Pomerance, this follows if for every fixed $δ>0$ there are $y^{1-o(1)}$ primes $p\le5y$ with $p+1$ free of prime factors exceeding $y^δ$. We write this implication out with explicit parameters and formalize it in Lean 4. We then check that the argument of the recent OpenAI preprint "Weighted dilation graphs, smooth shifted primes and totient fibers", which claims the corresponding statement for $p-1$, applies to $p+1$ after a change of sign in two of its sections. Consequently $h(x)=x^{2-o(1)}$, conditionally on the correctness of that preprint, which has not been refereed and whose main new estimates we have not independently verified.

We give a negative answer to the second question of Erdős Problem #1117: can the number $ν_f(r)$ of maximum-modulus points of a nonzero, non-monomial entire function on $|z|=r$ tend to infinity as $r\to\infty$? Write $f(z)=z^m g(z)$ with $g(0)\ne0$, and let $k$ be the first positive exponent with a nonzero coefficient in the Taylor expansion of $g$. We prove that $\{r>0:ν_f(r)>2k\}$ is locally finite in $(0,\infty)$, and that the constant $2k$ is sharp. In particular, $\liminf_{r\to\infty}ν_f(r)\le2k<\infty$, without a growth assumption. The proof combines finite local parametrizations of a logarithmic-derivative correspondence with analytic continuation and a local description of stationary points.
